planting.note: Plant in a warm, humid, part-shaded site with a trellis or support once nights stay reliably above 50°F; container culture with winter indoor protection is the safest route in zone 9a.

directions: This South American species is grown chiefly as a foliage specialty rather than for its small, pale greenish-cream flowers, since its three-lobed leaves are etched with bold purple-brown bands radiating along the veins and flushed purple underneath. Filtered or part-day light brings out the deepest leaf color and prevents scorching, while deep shade causes the banding to fade toward plain green. It is noticeably more cold-sensitive than the common hardy passionflowers, so Gulf Coast gardeners in zone 9a should plan on overwintering a potted vine indoors or treating it as a warm-season container specimen rather than leaving it to a permanent outdoor trellis.
sources: specialist Passiflora nursery cultivation notes (John Vanderplank, Passiflora Nursery)

planting.note: Plant on a sturdy trellis or fence in full sun after frost danger passes; established roots can be mulched heavily to carry the vine through a hard freeze.

directions: Native to the grasslands and forest margins of southern Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina, this vine produces large, fragrant white flowers with a dramatic corona banded in deep purple-blue, rivaling the familiar blue passionflower in beauty. It is markedly more cold-tolerant than most tender Passiflora species, typically dying back to the rootstock after a hard freeze and resprouting vigorously from the base once soil warms in spring, which makes it a reasonable gamble for a Gulf Coast zone 9a trellis where winter protection is impractical. Give it full sun and a sturdy support, since mature vines put on substantial growth in a single warm season.
sources: specialist Passiflora nursery cultivation notes (John Vanderplank, Passiflora Nursery)

planting.note: Plant in a warm, humid, sheltered site with filtered light and a support structure once temperatures stay reliably warm.

directions: This Amazon basin native is a collector's curiosity grown almost entirely for its singular leaf shape, a single asymmetrical curved lobe that gives each leaf the unmistakable silhouette of a shark's fin rather than the lobed or heart-shaped foliage typical of the genus. Its small greenish-white flowers are inconspicuous by comparison and easy to miss against the foliage. It wants warm, humid, part-shaded conditions similar to an understory vine and has no frost tolerance to speak of, so in zone 9a it is best suited to container culture with winter protection under glass rather than a permanent garden planting.
sources: specialist Passiflora nursery cultivation notes (John Vanderplank, Passiflora Nursery)

planting.note: Plant along a fence line or in a spot where vigorous reseeding can be tolerated or contained, in part sun and average soil.

directions: Named for its three-lobed leaves that resemble mulberry foliage, this fast-growing South American species bears small white-and-purple flowers followed by dark purple-black, marble-sized fruit that birds spread readily. It has naturalized along fence rows and woodland edges in parts of peninsular Florida, so Gulf Coast gardeners should treat it as a quick, vigorous fence or trellis cover rather than a restrained ornamental and should deadhead or remove fruit before it drops if volunteer seedlings are unwanted. It tolerates part shade better than most fruiting passionflowers, making it useful along a partly shaded property line.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant in a warm, humid, sheltered site with part shade and a trellis once all danger of frost has passed.

directions: Native to Mexico and Central America, this species takes its name from the dense, soft, velvety pubescence covering its broad, heart-shaped leaves and young stems, giving the foliage a tactile quality unusual in the genus. The greenish-cream flowers are modest and secondary to the plant's appeal as a foliage and texture specimen for a collector's trellis. It has no cold tolerance worth relying on, so Gulf Coast growers in zone 9a should plan on container culture with winter protection rather than a permanent outdoor planting.
sources: specialist Passiflora nursery cultivation notes (John Vanderplank, Passiflora Nursery)
